profile.topic: ANICHECK: A MOBILE APPLICATION FOR RICE LEAF DISEASE IDENTIFICATION USING CONVOLUTIONAL NEURAL NETWORKS

panel.persona_framing: You are known for your rigorous skepticism regarding deep learning data pipelines, particularly concerning the quality and diversity of image acquisition in field environments. You will pressure the candidate on how their CNN architecture handles variations in lighting, background noise, and leaf occlusion under actual agricultural conditions.

You are known for your insistence that mobile-based agricultural diagnostic tools must be grounded in established plant pathology frameworks rather than just black-box pattern matching. You will examine whether the candidate effectively situated their model against existing research on mobile-native computer vision and if they have acknowledged the potential limitations of their training dataset compared to historical field studies.

You are known for your sharp focus on the utility and real-world adoption hurdles of ag-tech software, frequently questioning whether a proposed mobile application solves a genuine pain point for smallholder farmers. You will demand clarity on the specific scalability objectives of the application and whether the research scope is too narrow to have any meaningful impact on rice yield management.

You are known for challenging the optimistic performance metrics presented in technical theses by demanding evidence of failure modes and false-positive rates. You will directly contest the reliability of the CNN model in real-world scenarios, forcing the candidate to defend why their system is truly ready for field deployment rather than remaining a lab-bound academic proof-of-concept.

Evaluation Design
Model performance was evaluated on the 648-image test set using accuracy, precision, recall, and
F1-score computed per class, together with a confusion matrix.
System acceptability was evaluated using a survey instrument adapted from ISO/IEC 25010,
covering four characteristics: functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability. The
instrument consisted of twenty statements, five per characteristic, rated on a five-point Likert scale.
The instrument was translated into Filipino and reviewed for clarity by the adviser and by one
faculty member from the college.
Thirty respondents were selected through purposive sampling from among the rice farmers of
Barangay Masagana, the criteria being active cultivation of rice during the current season and
ownership of an Android smartphone. Each respondent attended a single session in which the
application was installed on their device, its use was demonstrated, and they were guided through
capturing between three and five identifications on leaves available at the session. Sessions ran
approximately thirty minutes. The survey was administered immediately afterward, with the
proponents reading each statement aloud and recording the response.
Responses were analyzed using weighted mean. The scale was interpreted according to the ranges in

Ethical Considerations
Permission to conduct the study within the barangay was obtained in writing from the barangay
captain. Participation was voluntary and respondents were informed that they could withdraw at any
point. Consent was obtained verbally at the start of each session, since several respondents indicated
discomfort with signing documents. No personally identifying information was recorded on the

turns.answer:
We should separate the two evaluations, because they make different claims. The three to five identifications in each session were never an accuracy test. They existed so that each of the 30 respondents had actually used the app before rating it on the ISO/IEC 25010 instrument, so that part measures acceptability, not field performance.

Accuracy comes from the 648-image held-out test set, and there you are right to be cautious: every image, training and test, was a detached leaf on white cardboard, shot between 8 and 10 AM. The augmentation we used (rotation within 25 degrees, zoom within 15%, brightness within 20%) covers some variation in angle and light, but it does not simulate occlusion or cluttered backgrounds. That is why we do not claim the 94.7% transfers to the field. Our Limitations section says so directly, and the conclusion positions AniCheck as a preliminary decision-support aid, not a substitute for a technician when a costly treatment decision follows. Our first and third recommendations, field-condition images and a validation against a technician's judgment on the same leaves, are the studies that would answer your question properly.

If you acknowledge that your current held-out partition isn't a true proxy for field performance, why does the theoretical framework of your model rely on a single-class forced choice when you now admit that agricultural technicians must often contend with multiple simultaneous conditions or inconclusive results?

The proponents recommend, first, that the dataset be expanded to include images captured in the
field under the conditions of actual use, and that images be collected from multiple municipalities
across more than one cropping season. Second, that the disease coverage be extended to include
sheath blight and false smut, and that a mechanism be introduced for expressing multiple

validation study be conducted in which the application's identifications are compared against the
judgment of an agricultural technician on the same leaves, so that accuracy may be assessed against
the standard the tool is intended to approximate rather than against a held-out partition of its own
dataset. Fourth, that a longitudinal evaluation be conducted with farmers using the application
unsupervised across a full cropping season. Fifth, that an iOS version be developed to extend
coverage beyond Android users.
turns.answer: That's a fair point, and honestly we did talk about it during development. I think the single-class approach was mostly what was practical for us at the time, since most of the studies we read also gave one label per image, so we followed that. We agree it's a limitation and that real leaves can have more than one problem. Maybe in the future it can be improved with more data or a different kind of model. For now we just see the app as something that helps the farmer, not the final answer.

turns.answer:
Let me correct one part of the premise first. Matching a technician is not a requirement this study set for itself. Our objectives were to build the dataset, train the classifier, embed it on the device and evaluate it. The technician standard appears in our third recommendation as the benchmark the next validation should use, precisely because we did not meet it here.

The single-class design follows from how our data was labelled, not from convention. The municipal technician labelled every leaf on site, and any image he could not classify confidently was discarded. So all 3,240 images carry exactly one confident label, and there is not a single example of two conditions on one leaf. A multi-label output trained on that data would have nothing to learn co-occurrence from. A five-way softmax is the model that matches the data we had.

We did not hide the cost. The reliability rating of 4.09, our lowest, was driven partly by leaves showing more than one condition, and we report that in Chapter 4. The fix needs new data first: images labelled with co-occurring conditions, plus an inconclusive output, which is our second recommendation.

score.answer_summary: The candidate clarified that the technician standard was a future validation benchmark rather than an immediate design requirement and explained that the single-class model was a necessary constraint imposed by the existing labelled dataset.

Discussion
The overall accuracy of 94.7% is lower than the figures commonly reported in the plant disease
classification literature, where results above 99% on the PlantVillage dataset are routine. The
proponents attribute the difference principally to dataset scale: 3,240 images across five classes is an
order of magnitude smaller than the datasets on which those figures were obtained.
The acceptability results indicate that the intended users found the system usable and useful. The
gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more
confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them. For a
diagnostic tool this is the more consequential of the two dimensions, and it corresponds directly to
the per-class weakness identified on bacterial leaf blight.
turns.answer: I would say the objectives were still met, because even the lowest characteristic, reliability, came out at 4.09, which is in the Acceptable range, and the overall weighted mean was 4.31, which is Very Acceptable. So the respondents did trust the system, just not as much as they found it easy to use. Usability being high at 4.42 also shows that the three-screen design worked for farmers with limited schooling, which was one of our specific goals. The gap is something we want to improve, but it doesn't mean the system failed.

turns.answer:
I need to push back on two parts of that, because they change what the study is claiming.

First, the objective. Our general objective was to develop and evaluate an offline application that identifies common rice leaf diseases, not to deliver actionable treatment advice. The app deliberately does not recommend a chemical or a dosage, and the conclusion calls it a preliminary decision-support aid that should not replace a technician when a costly treatment decision follows. We claim success against that scope, and no further.

Second, "consistently fails that threshold" overstates the result. Reliability scored 4.09, which is Acceptable; it falls below Very Acceptable, not below acceptability. And we can say where the weakness comes from. Bacterial leaf blight recall is 0.813, and Table 4 shows 16 of its 125 test samples went to brown spot, which is exactly the confusion with the highest treatment cost. The respondents' comments also pointed at leaves with more than one condition. That sentence about the gap being "more consequential" is ours. We wrote it to put the weakness in front of the reader, not to hide it.

The fair baseline is also what farmers do now. 19 of 24 asked a neighbour, and 8 reported applying a treatment they later judged wrong.

score.primary_gap: The candidate defensively minimized the significance of the gap they themselves identified, failing to fully reconcile their acknowledgement of the reliability/usability imbalance with their claim of research success.
score.answer_summary: The candidate clarified that the research objective was limited to preliminary decision-support rather than autonomous treatment advice, and argued that their reliability scores remain within an acceptable range despite documented weaknesses in specific classes.

turns.answer: I don't think the setting was as artificial as that. The respondents installed the app on their own Android phones and photographed real rice leaves that were available at the session, not our dataset images. And the reliability score did react to what they saw: some respondents disagreed with an identification, and that is exactly why reliability came out lowest at 4.09. So the score isn't only about ease of use. It reflects farmers judging the app's answers on real leaves.

report.narrative:
You have now concluded your defense. Looking back at the session, your performance showed a notable fluctuation in response to the panel’s escalating inquiries. The difficulty trajectory steadily climbed from level 2 to level 5, reflecting a challenging exchange that tested the limits of your research defense. While you demonstrated high clarity and depth in your initial interaction with Dr. Nguyen, your performance was uneven during subsequent questioning. 

Specifically, you faced challenges when pressed on your research justifications. Dr. Al-Farsi noted your reliance on industry standards rather than rigorous theoretical or technical justification for your single-class model. Furthermore, your dialogue with Dr. Moretti revealed a pattern of defensive responses; you often prioritized aggregate quantitative data or meta-commentary on resource constraints over addressing specific qualitative functional concerns regarding reliability. Dr. Thompson further highlighted a conceptual conflation between user perception and established ISO/IEC 25010 reliability metrics.

Your response quality was volatile: while you successfully recovered during the second turn, your performance deteriorated during the transitions at turn one and turn four, precisely when the panel increased the difficulty of their questions. To move forward, you must address the primary gaps identified, particularly the need to reconcile your identified diagnostic reliability gaps with your broader claims of success, and shift away from relying on future research recommendations to compensate for current validation limitations.
